title: Common Core L.CCR.2 Explained
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Stuart glosses the Language strand's second anchor standard - command of capitalization, punctuation and spelling - and argues that conventions are not pedantry but gatekeeping. The move he makes is to reason from consequence backward for each convention rather than from the rule forward. Capitalization gets the 'cap-happy writer' diagnosis: students learn the basic rule and then over-apply it, so the instructional target is restraint and recognizing proper nouns. Punctuation gets the sharpest claim in the piece, that correct commas are downstream of syntax - a student who can tell a clause from a phrase and a subordinating from a coordinating conjunction places punctuation correctly almost as a by-product. Spelling gets a deliberately modest bar: not spelling-bee mastery but high-frequency homophones and a working grasp of English spelling patterns. His motivating image throughout is the employer's slush pile, where a cover letter with run-ons or misspellings goes to die. The one concrete routine he offers is having students keep a running list of their own personal 'spelling monsters' folded into a proofreading checklist, and he ends by asking readers for theirs.
points: Stuart teaches conventions from their consequences - the employer's slush pile rather than the rule book - which supplies the motivation a grammar worksheet cannot.
His diagnosis of the 'cap-happy' writer is an over-generalization problem: students learn a capitalization rule and apply it everywhere, so the lesson needed is restraint, not more rules.
He claims punctuation accuracy is a by-product of syntactic knowledge, so teaching clause-versus-phrase does more for comma placement than teaching comma rules does.
He sets a deliberately achievable spelling standard - high-frequency homophones plus spelling patterns - rather than treating spelling ability as a talent students either have or lack.
The transferable routine is the individualized 'spelling monsters' list attached to a proofreading checklist, which makes each student the owner of their own error pattern.
quotes: Have you ever taught a cap-happy writer? I'm guessing you have. They learn the basics of capitalization and then over-apply them to their writing.
C'mon, Thomas — capitalizing “course”? Really? Now that I'm finished ribbing a founding father, let's get to the point: college and career ready folks have got to be savvy cappers.
Nothing says, “Throw me into the slush pile,” to a prospective employer like a cover letter with a few run-ons or fragments. The college and career ready person dominates the heck out of punctuation.

They know, either instinctively or consciously, the difference between a clause and a phrase, between a subordinating and a coordinating conjunction, between a dependent and an independent clause. Because of their working knowledge of how sentences function, they are able to appropriately place commas and periods and the rest of the punctuation gang.

All right, maybe there is something else that says, “Throw me in the slush pile, please” — misspellings. You don't necessarily need to be a Scripps champion to be college and career ready, but you do need to be able to correctly spell high-frequency homophones and have a strong grasp of the spelling patterns of English. There are lots of great ways to do this; in my high school classes, I have students keep a list of their own personal “spelling monsters” and I include this on their proofreading checklist.
